(CNN) -- Sen. Hillary Clinton will stop telling an emotional story about a uninsured pregnant woman who died after being denied medical care, Clinton's campaign said. Sen. Hillary Clinton was repeating a story she heard from someone on the campaign trail. A hospital has raised questions over the accuracy of the story, and Clinton's campaign has said although they had no reason to doubt the story, they were unable to confirm the details. In the story, Clinton describes a woman from rural Ohio who was making minimum wage at a local pizza shop. The woman, who was uninsured, became pregnant. Clinton said the woman ran into trouble and went to a hospital in a nearby county but was denied treatment because she couldn't afford a $100 payment. In her speeches, Clinton said the woman later was taken to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The young woman was then taken by helicopter to a Columbus hospital where she died of complications.  Watch why the story is raising questions » . The New York senator heard the story during a campaign visit to a family's living room in Pomeroy, Ohio, in late February. Bryan Holman was hosting the candidate and told Clinton the story. She has repeated it frequently since then. As recently as Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said she was "just aching inside" as she was listening to the story. "It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn't have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined," she said. While Clinton never named the hospital in her speech, the woman she was referring to was treated at O'Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman did indeed have insurance, and, at least at their hospital, she was never turned away. Hospital Chief Executive Officer Rick Castrop in a statement said, "we reviewed the medical and patient accounts of the patient" after she was named in a newspaper story about Clinton's stump speech. "There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman." A hospital spokesperson confirmed to CNN the woman had insurance. She said the hospital decided to come forward after people in the community began to question if they had denied her care. Clinton's speech accurately reflects what she was told that day, but the campaign admits they were not able to confirm the account. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said, "She had no reason to doubt his word." "Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it's common for candidates to retell those stories. It's not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren't able to fully vet the story," he said. Elleithee added, "If the hospital claims it didn't happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won't repeat the story." "She never mentions the hospital by name and isn't trying to cast blame. She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That's a point very few people will dispute." E-mail to a friend .

# Clinton Campaign Drops Disputed Health Care Anecdote

Senator Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign announced it will no longer repeat an emotionally charged story about an uninsured pregnant woman who allegedly died after being denied medical treatment, following challenges to the account's accuracy.

Clinton first heard the story in late February during a campaign stop in Pomeroy, Ohio, where she visited a family in their living room as part of her outreach efforts. It was there that a man named Bryan Holman shared the tragic tale with her. Moved by the story, Clinton began incorporating it into her stump speeches, using it as a powerful illustration of the human cost of America's health care system and the dangers faced by uninsured Americans.

According to the version of events Clinton relayed on the campaign trail, the woman worked a minimum-wage job at a pizza shop in rural Ohio and lacked health insurance. Clinton claimed the woman was turned away from a hospital because she could not afford an upfront payment of $100. Sometime afterward, Clinton said, the woman lost her baby and ultimately died as a result of complications tied to the denied care.

However, the story quickly came under scrutiny once it reached the hospital named in connection with the woman's treatment. O'Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio, pushed back publicly against the narrative, stating that the woman in question had, in fact, been insured at the time and was never refused treatment or turned away from their facility. The hospital's account directly contradicted the central details Clinton had been sharing with audiences across the state and beyond.

Faced with this discrepancy, the Clinton campaign issued a statement acknowledging the situation. Campaign representatives said they had no initial reason to question the truthfulness of Holman's account when Clinton first heard it, but conceded that they had not been able to independently verify the specific details before Clinton began repeating it publicly. Given the hospital's firm rebuttal and the campaign's inability to substantiate the story through further investigation, officials decided the responsible course of action was to stop telling it altogether.

The episode highlights the risks candidates face when incorporating personal anecdotes shared by voters into their campaign messaging, particularly when such stories involve sensitive and emotionally resonant issues like health care access. While the intent behind sharing the story may have been to humanize policy debates, the inconsistencies that emerged underscore the importance of verification before such narratives are amplified on a national stage.

# Clinton Campaign Drops Uninsured Woman's Story After Hospital Disputes Account

Senator Hillary Clinton has been a frequent and passionate advocate for health care reform throughout her presidential campaign, often illustrating the human cost of America's insurance gaps with personal anecdotes gathered from voters she met on the campaign trail. One story in particular became a fixture of her stump speech: the tragic account of a pregnant woman in Ohio who allegedly died after being turned away from a hospital because she could not immediately produce a $100 payment.

According to Clinton, she first heard the story from a family in Pomeroy, Ohio, a small town in the southeastern part of the state. In her retelling, the woman, who lacked health insurance, sought care at a local hospital while pregnant but was refused treatment when she was unable to pay the requested fee upfront. Clinton used the anecdote as a powerful, visceral example of the human toll of the nation's health care crisis, arguing that no one in America should die simply because they could not afford $100 for medical treatment.

The story resonated with audiences and became one of Clinton's go-to examples in making the case for her health care reform proposals, which called for near-universal coverage. She repeated the account at multiple campaign stops, presenting it as a real and urgent illustration of why reform was necessary.

However, the narrative began to unravel after officials at O'Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio—the hospital believed to be connected to the story—came forward to dispute key details of Clinton's account. Hospital representatives stated publicly that the woman in question had, in fact, been insured at the time and had never been denied medical care or turned away due to inability to pay. This directly contradicted the central claims of the story Clinton had been telling voters.

Faced with the hospital's public rebuttal, Clinton's campaign was forced to respond. After conducting its own review, the campaign acknowledged that it had been unable to independently verify the specific details of the story as Clinton had presented them. As a result, campaign officials announced that Clinton would discontinue telling the anecdote on the campaign trail going forward.

The episode highlighted the risks candidates face when incorporating personal stories and anecdotes—often gathered informally from constituents and supporters—into their campaign rhetoric. While such stories can be powerful tools for connecting policy arguments to real human experiences, they also carry the risk of factual inaccuracies that can undermine a candidate's credibility if not properly vetted before being repeated publicly. The incident became a minor but notable episode in the broader debate over health care policy that defined much of the 2008 Democratic presidential primary.

- Others have contended that scrutiny intensified unfairly during her presidential campaigns
- Media analysts have studied how coverage patterns shifted between her different roles

The relationship between CNN and Clinton reflects broader patterns in how 24-hour news networks cover major political figures who occupy the news cycle for extended periods. Her transition from Senator to Secretary of State to presidential candidate meant that CNN's editorial approach had to adapt to covering her in different capacities—as a legislator, a diplomat, and eventually as a candidate for the nation's highest office.

## Conclusion

Understanding CNN's coverage of Hillary Clinton, particularly during her Senate years, provides valuable insight into how modern political journalism operates. This case study remains relevant for media studies scholars examining the evolution of political coverage in the cable news era.

Hillary Clinton had shared the story in recent campaign appearances as an illustrative example while discussing her policy priorities, describing an encounter she said underscored the human stakes of the issue. The dispute is the latest example of a campaign anecdote facing pushback after public retelling, a recurring hazard for candidates who rely on personal stories to humanize policy arguments. A hospital spokesperson said administrators felt compelled to speak up once the story began circulating widely, saying they wanted to "set the record straight" on what their internal records showed. The hospital did not accuse Clinton of intentionally misrepresenting events, but said the details as recounted did not match their documentation.

Clinton allies downplayed the significance of the discrepancy, noting that campaign anecdotes are often drawn from memory and can be imprecise in specifics even when they reflect a broader truth the candidate is trying to convey. Critics, however, seized on the episode as fodder for questions about Clinton's candor, a theme that has dogged her candidacy at various points.

Republican opponents were quick to highlight the retraction. A spokesperson for one rival campaign said the episode "raises questions" about Clinton's reliability in recounting her own experiences, while Democratic strategists cautioned against reading too much into what they characterized as a minor dispute over a single anecdote.

The Clinton campaign emphasized that the substance of her policy argument remains unchanged, even though the specific story will no longer be part of her stump speech repertoire. "The point she was making stands," the spokesperson said. "But out of respect for the hospital and its patients, she won't be using that particular story going forward."
